# A first marathon: a 18-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 27 October 2026 from 25 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

26.2 miles (42.2 km) of running. [1, 2]

**Before this plan:** If you cannot yet run for 30 minutes without stopping, do the NHS Couch to 5K first: it ends with 30-minute runs three times a week. [3, 4]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [4, 5]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 4]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [6, 7, 8]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [4, 9]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [8, 10]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 8]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [4, 8, 11]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 3, 12]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [8, 13, 14]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. The Saturday long run is the key session: at an easy, conversational pace; walking breaks are fine.

*Steady run*: a run at a comfortably steady effort, about 5 to 6 out of 10, for 30 to 45 minutes. 

## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [3, 12]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 12]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [3]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [11, 14]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [4, 14]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 3, 12]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 15]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [14, 15]
- Train in the footwear you will use on the day and break new shoes in gradually. Wear moisture-wicking socks and change them if your feet sweat. [11, 14, 16]
- Deal with a hot spot as soon as you feel it. Cover a blister with a soft or padded plaster and do not burst it; get advice if it shows signs of infection. [11, 16]

## On the day

- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [6, 14]

## Safety

- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [17]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [18]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [4, 14]
